chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
title: Later record labels and her string and orchestral albums
summary: Besides Capitol she recorded for Decca, Columbia, Imperial and Liberty, including sung-only albums with Russ Garcia and Harold Mooney and some Billy May sessions.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: today why I'm not -- they don't hear more of me. Well, the answer is, you know, I've been with several record companies. Capitol, of course, was my first company. And then I was with Decca awhile and I was with Columbia, and I did some things for Imperial and one of the things that I did was on Liberty. I did an album on Liberty which I consider a very, very good album, with Russ Garcia doing the arranging for me on that album, and he did a marvelous job. It's a marvelous album. It was one of the -- one of the few things, I suppose, that I did where I didn't play. I didn't play the piano at all on that particular album. But I just vocalized and just concentrated on vocalizing. And also on the Capitol thing I did a session where I didn't play, and that also, that was Harold Mooney did the arrangements on that, and that was a session that I was quite proud of also, because you know, I was experimenting with something different you see, getting away from the completely rhythm things. And of course this was what Nat did. It's the same pattern almost that Nat King Cole -- that they followed with Nat King Cole, you see.

But I was glad to -- it gave me a chance to really display some versatility, you know, because I could perform as a single artist or with -- when I say single I mean with rhythm and piano, and/or with a big orchestra. That was -- but the arrangements were built around me and for me, and I give -- really, I give both of these men credit. Harold Mooney on

Capitol.

Also, Billy May didn't do a bad job. I did some things with him on Capitol, although this is sort of coming to me in the --Billy May was also a very wonderful man, very wonderful. I did some things with him too, but the things with Harold Mooney were a little different, because that was my time to experiment with strings, you know, which sort of gave a little -- a little something extra, you know, to what I'd done, and I'm very proud of that.
